# tsuzuri

A personal blog: a portrait and bio on the home page, and posts underneath.
Each post can carry more than one translation, and a reader is served
whichever translation best matches the locales their browser sends.

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
```

## Commands

| Command                | What it does                                              |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run dev`           | Serves the site locally with hot reload.                   |
| `npm run build`         | Builds the production bundle.                              |
| `npm run start`         | Serves a build produced by `npm run build`.                |
| `npm run format`        | Rewrites the project in place to its house style.          |
| `npm run format:check`  | Reports formatting drift without rewriting anything.       |
| `npm run lint`          | Lints the whole project; also checks formatting.           |
| `npm run typecheck`     | Type-checks the project. The test runner compiles without checking types, so this is the only thing that does. |
| `npm test`              | Runs the unit test suite.                                  |
| `npm run test:e2e`      | Runs the end-to-end suite. Builds the app and serves it first, so it needs a browser — `npx playwright install chromium` once per machine. |

## Layout

- `app/(site)/` — the reader-facing route group: the home page, the post
  detail page, and the small data module they both read from.
- `shared/` — code shared by more than one part of the app, independent of any
  one route. `shared/resolve-translation.ts` is the locale-fallback logic a
  post detail page calls into; `shared/blog-post-slug.ts` is the slug shape
  every post's `slug` is validated against.
- `shared/*.spec.ts` — unit tests, colocated with the code they cover.
- `e2e/` — end-to-end specs, kept apart from the unit tests above because they
  exercise the whole running app rather than one module in isolation.
- `docs/` — operational notes that do not belong in code comments, such as
  [deployment](docs/deployment.md).
- `.github/workflows/` — the checks that run on every pull request.

## Contributing

Changes go through a pull request rather than landing straight on `main`.
Before writing code, sketch the plan and get it approved — this catches a
misunderstood requirement while it is still cheap to redirect, rather than
after the diff exists. A pull request is reviewed by someone other than the
person who wrote it, and merges only once that review is clean and the checks
above pass.

3	/**
4	 * The post catalog. It is checked in and compiled into the build. Reading it
5	 * from a content backend instead is a later change.

7	export const POSTS: readonly Post[] = [

9			slug: "hello-world",
10			defaultLocale: "ja-JP",
11			translations: [
12				{
13					locale: "ja-JP",
14					title: "はじめまして",

16				},

20					body: "A short note about this blog.",
21				},
22			],
23		},
24		{
25			slug: "on-writing-in-two-languages",
26			defaultLocale: "ja-JP",
27			translations: [
28				{
29					locale: "ja",
30					title: "二言語で書くということ",
31					body: "日本語と英語で書く理由について。",
32				},
33			],
34		},

36			slug: "draft-notes",
37			defaultLocale: "ja-JP",

39			translations: [],

43	/** The post whose slug is `slug`, or `undefined` when the catalog has none. */
44	export function findPostBySlug(slug: string): Post | undefined {
45		return POSTS.find((post) => post.slug === slug);
46	}

1	import { z } from "zod";
2	
3	/** Upper bound on a post slug's length, enforced by the schema below. */
4	export const MAX_SLUG_LENGTH = 96;
5	
6	/**
7	 * Shape of a post slug: lowercase alphanumeric groups joined by single
8	 * hyphens, with no leading, trailing, or doubled hyphen. A slug becomes part
9	 * of a URL path and a cache key, so it is validated before either is built
10	 * from it rather than trusted as-is.
11	 */
12	export const PostSlug = z
13		.string()
14		.min(1)
15		.max(MAX_SLUG_LENGTH)
16		.regex(/^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$/);
17	
18	export type PostSlug = z.infer<typeof PostSlug>;
19	
20	/** Message shown next to a slug field that failed {@link PostSlug}. */
21	export const SLUG_VALIDATION_MESSAGE =
22		"Use lowercase letters, numbers, and single hyphens (e.g. my-post-title).";

# Deployment

Operational notes for running this site outside a local checkout. `npm run
build` produces what is served and `npm run start` serves it; everything below
is what a real deployment target adds around that pair.

## Environments

| Environment | Trigger                     | Notes                            |
| ----------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Production  | Push to `main`              | Serves the default locale first. |
| Preview     | Pull request opened/updated | One preview per pull request.    |

## Locale fallback

A reader's accepted locales come from their browser's `Accept-Language`
header. `shared/resolve-translation.ts` is what turns that preference list
into the translation a post detail page renders — see its own documentation
for the exact resolution order. Deployment does not change that order; it only
changes which posts and translations the deployed build carries.

## Rolling back

Redeploy the previous commit's build. There is no database to migrate back —
the post catalog and everything else the app reads live in the build itself —
so a rollback here is just a redeploy.

content.text:
## Proposal: reader corrections on a post

### What a reader sees

At the bottom of the post article (`app/(site)/posts/[slug]/page.tsx`), a small form: one textarea for the correction and a submit button. No account, no required contact info. On submit, it replaces itself with a short confirmation ("Thanks, I'll take a look") or an inline error — no page navigation.

### What we capture

- The post's `slug`.
- The `locale` of the translation the reader was actually looking at (i.e. whatever `resolveTranslation` picked for them) — not the post's `defaultLocale`, since what needs fixing is specific to the translation they read.
- The correction text itself, free-text, length-bounded (say 20–2000 characters) — one field, not a structured "typo / broken link / other" picker, matching what you asked for.
- Nothing else. No name/email field for v1 — it lowers friction, and this is a low-stakes, low-volume personal blog rather than a support inbox that needs a reply channel.

Validation for that shape belongs in `shared/`, as a small zod schema (`shared/post-correction.ts`, alongside `shared/blog-post-slug.ts`) — both the form and whatever handles the submission need the same rule, so it can't live only at one call site.

### Where a submission goes

This is the one real architectural decision, because the project currently has **no datastore at all** — `docs/deployment.md` states that explicitly as a feature ("no database to migrate back"). Two ways to handle that:

1. **Forward it out, store nothing.** A Next.js Server Action (co-located with the post route, e.g. `app/(site)/posts/[slug]/submit-correction.ts`) validates the payload and forwards it to an outbound notification — email or a webhook (e.g. Slack/Discord) — so it lands wherever you already read messages. Nothing new to back up, migrate, or roll back; failure mode is "the notification didn't arrive," not "we lost data."
2. **Persist it.** Write to a hosted DB/KV so corrections are listable somewhere. This means picking and provisioning a datastore, which is a bigger change than the feature itself and cuts against how this project is deliberately built (static content compiled into the build, redeploy = rollback).

I'd go with **(1)**. It keeps the site's shape intact and is proportionate to "let readers flag a typo." If you later want a dashboard of open corrections, that's a natural follow-up PR once you know how much volume there actually is.

Concretely: a Server Action posts to an email API (I'd default to Resend, since it's the common pairing with Next.js, but any transactional-email or webhook provider works) with the post slug, locale, and correction text. **This needs a real account and an API key/secret before it can send anything** — that's an operational step for you, not something I can wire up blind. In dev/test, the send is stubbed out (see testing, below) so nothing real goes out.

### Abuse handling

Kept minimal, proportionate to a personal blog:
- A honeypot field (hidden, filled only by bots) — if set, silently drop the submission without an error.
- Length cap on the correction text (already covered by the shared schema).
- No CAPTCHA, no auth, no rate limiting store — a rate limiter needs somewhere to keep counters, which is the same "no datastore" tension as above. If spam turns out to be a real problem, that's a scoped follow-up.

### Testing

- `shared/post-correction.spec.ts` — unit tests for the validation schema (empty text, over-length text, missing slug, valid case), same pattern as `shared/blog-post-slug.spec.ts`.
- An e2e spec exercising the form on a post page: fill it in, submit, see the confirmation state. The outbound email/webhook call needs to be stubbed for e2e/CI — either via an env var the Server Action checks (`CORRECTIONS_WEBHOOK_URL` unset → log instead of send) or a small seam the test can point at a local stub server. I'd lean toward the env-var-unset-means-noop approach since it needs no test-only code path in the handler itself.

### Out of scope for this change

- No moderation UI, no listing of past corrections anywhere in the app.
- No reader-visible history ("3 people flagged this").
- No reply-to-reader flow (no email collected).
- No changes to `resolve-translation.ts` — the form only reads which translation was already resolved.

### Suggested PR split

1. `shared/post-correction.ts` + its spec — the validation schema alone.
2. The form UI + Server Action + outbound send (stubbed via env var) + e2e test.

That keeps "the shape of the data" reviewable separately from "how we act on it," and each PR stays small enough to actually review.

---

Biggest open item before anyone writes code: **pick the outbound destination** (which email/webhook provider, and whose inbox/channel it lands in) — I proposed Resend + a plain notification email as the default, but that's the one part of this plan that needs an account and a secret from you rather than a judgment call I can make in code.
